statement: Given a matrix A in R^{m x n}, the pseudoinverse of A (also known as the Moore–Penrose inverse, denoted by A^+) is the n x m matrix satisfying all four Penrose conditions: (1) A A^+ A = A, (2) A^+ A A^+ = A^+, (3) (A A^+)^* = A A^+, and (4) (A^+ A)^* = A^+ A, where * denotes the conjugate transpose.

properties.property: For any matrix A, the Moore–Penrose inverse A^+ is unique, and when A is non-singular, A^+ = A^{-1}
properties.why: all four Penrose conditions uniquely determine A^+, coinciding with the regular inverse when non-singular
the pseudoinverse is obtained from the singular-value decomposition A = U \begin{bmatrix} \Sigma_1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} V^{\operatorname{T}} by setting parameters X = Y = Z = 0
product relation between a {1,4}-inverse, A, and a {1,3}-inverse yields the Moore–Penrose inverse

assumptions.assumption: A is a matrix over a field (such as R^{m x n}) equipped with conjugate transposition and singular-value decomposition
assumptions.breaks_when: Generalizing to arbitrary algebraic structures like semigroups or rings where generalized inverses may not exist for some elements (e.g., element 2 in Z/12Z)

failure_modes.mode: Absence of generalized inverse in general algebraic structures
failure_modes.signature: No element b exists satisfying a * b * a = a
failure_modes.cause: Structure lacks required division or field properties, as seen with element 2 in Z/12Z

failure_modes.signature: A A^+ != I_m or A^+ A != I_n
failure_modes.cause: Matrix A is rectangular (m != n) or singular (det(A) = 0), meaning A lacks a regular two-sided inverse

failure_modes.mode: Singularity in one-sided inverse closed-form formulas
failure_modes.signature: Non-invertibility of A A^T or A^T A
failure_modes.cause: Matrix A lacks full row rank (rank(A) < m) for the right inverse formula A^T (A A^T)^{-1}, or lacks full column rank (rank(A) < n) for the left inverse formula (A^T A)^{-1} A^T
